beats.narration: This is Gerald. Gerald is a fern. And Gerald is about to die of neglect, for the third time this year.
Who watered Gerald? Somebody tell me somebody watered Gerald.
I thought you were watering Gerald.
I was at a conference. Gerald was your responsibility, Cy.
Gerald survives, barely. But in that moment, a very bad idea and a very good idea arrive at the same time.
What if the pot watered itself? A little computer that checks the soil and pours water when it is thirsty.
That is the good idea. The bad idea is Cy saying it will ship by spring.
We have never built a product. We have a fern, a soldering iron, and a lot of confidence.
Over this series, these three are going to build Sprout from a blinking light to a connected device in thousands of homes.
Along the way, you will learn how real embedded systems are designed, debugged, and shipped. No prior hardware experience required.
Okay, Ada. Explain it like I am an investor. What is an embedded system?

title.sub: What Even Is an Embedded System?

beats.narration: It is a computer that is built into something else, to do one job. Nobody thinks of it as a computer.
Your microwave has one. So does your car door, your remote, and probably your toothbrush.
My toothbrush has a computer? It still can't make me floss.
A laptop is a general-purpose machine. You can install anything on it. An embedded system is the opposite: it is purpose-built.
The device has one program, written for that exact hardware. When it powers on, that program runs, and it never stops.
Kilobytes? My phone wallpaper is bigger than that.
Your wallpaper is not responsible for keeping Gerald alive.
The heart of most embedded systems is a microcontroller: a single chip with a processor, memory, and input-output pins all packed together.
The processor reads instructions from flash, keeps its working data in RAM, and talks to the world through pins and peripherals.
Peripherals are like little helpers built into the chip. A timer counts. An analog converter measures voltages. A serial port talks to other chips.
Sprout needs to sense the soil, decide, and act. Sense, decide, act. Almost every embedded system is some version of that loop.
Sense, decide, act. I can sell that. I can put that on a hoodie.
There is one more ingredient that makes embedded work feel different: time. Many devices must respond not just correctly, but on time.
An airbag that inflates one second late is not slow, it is wrong. That is a hard real-time system. Late equals failure.
A music gadget that slips a few milliseconds sounds sloppy, but nobody gets hurt. That is softer.
Sprout is gentle. If it waters a minute late, Gerald will not notice.
But the same chip may also need to stop the pump the instant the water tank runs dry. Even gentle devices have a few sharp deadlines.
So, part of the job is finding which parts of the system are truly time critical, and protecting those first.
And the rest?
The rest can wait politely in line.
Embedded systems also tend to run unattended for years. Nobody reboots a thermostat for fun.
The code must recover from glitches on its own, because there is rarely a human nearby to press a button.
The next morning, Ben has a development board on the bench, a bare circuit board with a microcontroller on it. Ada has a laptop. Cy has a coffee.
So you write the program on the laptop and it just... runs on the little board?
Not quite. The laptop and the chip speak different machine languages. So we cross-compile.
We write C on the laptop. A cross compiler turns it into instructions for the chip, not for the laptop.
Then a programmer tool copies that image into the chip's flash.
That separation matters. The machine that builds the code is not the machine that runs it. Your laptop is the host. The board is the target.
And the target does not have a screen, or a keyboard, or a file system. It barely has an opinion.
Building the image takes a few steps. The compiler turns each C file into an object file.
The linker stitches them together and decides exactly where every function and variable lives in the chip's memory.
Then there is startup code, a few lines that run before main. They set up the stack, copy starting values into RAM, and zero the rest.
Only then does your program begin.
So main is not really the beginning?
Main is the beginning of your story. The chip had a whole prologue you never saw.
The linker can also write a map file, a report of where everything ended up and how big it is. It looks boring.
Later in this series, it will save the day.
Why C? It is close to the hardware, it is small, and nearly every chip vendor supports it. C plus plus, Rust, and even small Python variants exist too.
The trade-off is always control versus convenience.
Pick whatever ships fastest.

beats.narration: That is not how languages work, but I will take it as a vote for C.

beats.narration: Ada flashes the first program. Nothing happens. No error message. No crash dialog. Just a board, sitting there, doing nothing in particular.
Is it broken? Did we break it? It cost nine dollars!
This is the part nobody tells you about. When embedded code fails, it fails silently. There is no screen to print to.
So we give ourselves windows. First, an LED. If the light blinks, the code is running. Crude, but it works at three in the morning.

visual.title: Ways to see inside
items: Measure pins with a meter or scope

beats.narration: Second, a serial port. The chip sends text, one character at a time, over a wire to the laptop. It is the embedded version of a print statement.

visual.title: Ways to see inside
items: Measure pins with a meter or scope

beats.narration: Third, and best, a hardware debugger. It connects to special pins on the chip and lets you pause the processor, step through code line by line, and peek at memory.

visual.title: Ways to see inside
items: Measure pins with a meter or scope

beats.narration: With a debugger, I can stop the world and ask: what is in this variable right now? Which line are we on?
Then why does anybody blink LEDs?
Because debuggers change timing. Stop a chip that is controlling a motor, and the motor does not stop with it. Sometimes you need to watch without touching.
Ada steps through the code and finds it in four minutes. The program was waiting for a button that does not exist yet.
In fairness, I did say I would add the button tomorrow.
The lesson is bigger than a missing button. Debugging embedded systems is detective work. You form a theory, design a test that could prove it wrong, and run it.
The worst thing you can do is change five things at once. If it starts working, you do not know why, and it will break again on demo day.

visual.title: Detective method
items: Change one thing at a time

beats.narration: And when it is a hardware problem, the code can be perfect and still fail. A loose wire looks exactly like a software bug.

visual.title: Detective method
items: Change one thing at a time

beats.narration: So when something breaks, I should blame Ben's wires.

visual.title: Detective method
items: Change one thing at a time

beats.narration: When something breaks, you should bring snacks and stay out of the way.

beats.narration: Embedded engineers work under constraints that would make a web developer weep. Memory is measured in kilobytes. Every component costs money. And everything burns power.
Three dollars? I told the investors three dollars? Who let me talk to investors?
If you build a hundred thousand units, every cent on the parts list is a thousand dollars.
So we pick the smallest chip that does the job, with some room to grow.
Room to grow is the trick. Pick a chip with exactly enough memory, and the first new feature will not fit.
Pick one far too big, and you pay for silicon you never use.
Power is the other budget. A chip that runs flat out will drain two batteries in days. One that naps between jobs can last months.
These constraints shape every decision in the series ahead: how we structure code, how we talk to sensors, how we handle math, even when the chip is allowed to be awake.
There is a hidden cost too: engineering time. A bigger chip costs more per unit, but squeezing code into a tiny chip can cost months of effort.
For a product that sells a few hundred units, engineering time dominates, so a roomier chip is usually smarter. For millions of units, every cent of parts wins.
Know which kind of product you are building.
Before we write real code, I want us to agree on a few rules. Not laws. Habits that save you at three in the morning.
First, design so pieces can be tested on their own, even on the laptop, without the board.

visual.title: Habits that save you
items: Make it testable from day one
Write down why, not just what
Check every assumption on the real board

beats.narration: Second, keep the code in separate modules with clear jobs. The part that reads the soil should not care how the pump works.

visual.title: Habits that save you
items: Make it testable from day one
Write down why, not just what
Check every assumption on the real board

beats.narration: Third, document the why. Six months from now, nobody remembers why there is a mysterious delay of twelve milliseconds in the pump code.

visual.title: Habits that save you

Check every assumption on the real board

beats.narration: Fourth, the hardware will change. Boards get revised. Chips go out of stock. Code that is tied to one exact pin layout will hurt.

visual.title: Habits that save you

Write down why, not just what
Check every assumption on the real board

beats.narration: Fifth, ship by spring.

Check every assumption on the real board

beats.narration: Fifth, measure on the real board. A simulation is a hypothesis. The board is the truth.

beats.narration: Every product starts as a prototype. And prototypes start on development boards: cheap, friendly boards with a microcontroller, a USB port, and pins broken out for experiments.
Behold. A dev board, a moisture probe, a pump from an aquarium shop, and forty jumper wires.

beats.narration: It looks like a bowl of spaghetti that learned electricity.

visual.title: Prototype ladder

beats.narration: That is fine. A prototype answers questions fast. Does the sensor read wet and dry soil differently? Can this pump lift water high enough?

visual.title: Prototype ladder

beats.narration: The trap is falling in love with the prototype. Hobby boards are great for learning, but a product needs its own board: smaller, cheaper, and designed to survive real homes.

visual.title: Prototype ladder
items: Custom board, the one that ships

beats.narration: So we use the dev board to learn, and plan for our own board later. And we write code that will survive the move.

visual.title: Prototype ladder

beats.narration: Which is exactly what the next episode is about: architecture. How to organize code so the hardware can change underneath it.

beats.narration: One last truth before we go. In an embedded team, hardware and software are built in parallel, and they meet in the middle.
That meeting is called bring-up, and it is rarely calm.
Boards take weeks to manufacture. If Ada waits for my board before writing code, we lose a month.
So I write code against a plan: which pins, which sensors, which chip. I test it on the dev board and on my laptop.
When the real board arrives, most of the code is already waiting.
That only works if the two halves talk constantly. A pin that moves on the schematic must move in the code. A sensor that changes must change the driver.
So the secret to hardware startups is... talking to each other?
Shocking, I know. Also, schedules. Hardware is always later than the plan.
So, a recap. An embedded system is a dedicated computer hiding inside a product.
